\chapter{Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow}
\label{ch:ml-days}
\hlchaptermodality{94}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say which day something happened on or will happen on.}

From cold: the three day words, the three verb endings they travel with, and the observation that one of the three was already owned but locked inside a farewell.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[innŭ]{\ml{ഇന്ന്} (innŭ) — today}

\label{lesson:ML-C94-innu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{day}. You have had the word for a day since early on. You have never had a word for \textbf{this} one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} — \emph{innŭ} — \textbf{today.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകുന്നു}.} — \emph{innŭ ñān pōkunnu} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Today} I go.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The word goes \textbf{in front}, before the person and the verb. That is where a time word sits in this language, and you have been putting things there since you learned to say \emph{now}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
This is smaller than it looks and it opens more than it looks.

Every sentence you have made so far has floated free of any particular day. You could say that you go, that you went, that you will go — and nothing in the sentence said \textbf{when}. A listener had to guess from the room.

\textbf{One word ends that.} The verb was already carrying the tense; \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} gives it a day to sit on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{innŭ}
  \item \emph{innŭ ñān pōkunnu}
  \item where in the sentence the time word stands
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{today}? (\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}}.) Where does it go in the sentence? (\textbf{In front}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[innale]{\ml{ഇന്നലെ} (innale) — yesterday}

\label{lesson:ML-C94-innale}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{today}. Then say \emph{I went} — the past of the verb you have used most.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്നലെ}} — \emph{innale} — \textbf{yesterday.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്നലെ} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോയി}.} — \emph{innale ñān pōyi} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Yesterday} I went.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Put the two words side by side and read the fronts:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} \emph{innŭ} & today \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്നലെ}} \emph{innale} & yesterday \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{They begin the same way.} Yesterday is today with something added on the end — which is the direction this language has been growing words in all along, and here it is doing it to a day.

\begin{cousinweb}
You do not have to take it apart to use it, and you should not force a story onto the tail. \textbf{What is worth seeing is the shared front}, because it is what will make the pair easy to keep apart from \emph{tomorrow}, which begins somewhere else entirely.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{innŭ}, then \emph{innale}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{innale ñān pōyi}
  \item \emph{Look:} at the two words and find where they stop matching
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{yesterday}? (\textbf{\ml{ഇന്നലെ}}.) What does it share with \emph{today}? (\textbf{Its opening}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāḷe ñān pōkuṁ]{\ml{നാളെ} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും} (nāḷe ñān pōkuṁ) — tomorrow I will go}

\label{lesson:ML-C94-three-days}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{today} and \emph{yesterday}. Then say the goodbye you learned in your first week — the one that promises to see somebody again.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a word walks out of a phrase}]
You have owned \textbf{\ml{നാളെ}} since that goodbye. \textbf{\ml{നാളെ} \ml{കാണാം}} — see you tomorrow. Until now it has lived only there, glued to the seeing.

Take it out and stand it in front of a sentence of your own:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{നാളെ} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}.} — \emph{nāḷe ñān pōkuṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Tomorrow} I will go.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Nothing had to be learned to do that.} The word was in your mouth, the position was the one you gave \emph{today} two lessons ago, and the verb was already yours. A fixed phrase was holding a word that could stand on its own.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three days, three endings, one shape}]
Now put the three together and watch what moves:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്നലെ} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോയി}} & \emph{innale ñān pōyi} & yesterday I went \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകുന്നു}} & \emph{innŭ ñān pōkunnu} & today I go \\
\textbf{\ml{നാളെ} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}} & \emph{nāḷe ñān pōkuṁ} & tomorrow I will go \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The middle of every line is identical.} Only two things change, and they change together: the day word at the front, and the ending on the verb at the back.

The day word does not make the tense — the verb was doing that before you had any of these words. What the day word does is \textbf{say which day}, and the two agreeing is what a listener hears as an ordinary sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{innale ñān pōyi}
  \item \emph{innŭ ñān pōkunnu}
  \item \emph{nāḷe ñān pōkuṁ}
  \item the three lines again, and name what is the same in all of them
  \item where you first met the word for tomorrow
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which phrase had been holding \emph{tomorrow}? (\textbf{\ml{നാളെ} \ml{കാണാം}}.) What changes between the three lines? (\textbf{The day word and the verb ending}.) What carries the tense? (\textbf{The verb}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mūnnŭ divasaṁ enna ōrmma]{(yesterday, today, tomorrow) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R94-day-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Name the day you are standing in, and the one behind it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the three lines}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്നലെ} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോയി}} & yesterday I went \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകുന്നു}} & today I go \\
\textbf{\ml{നാളെ} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}} & tomorrow I will go \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read straight down the middle: \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} three times, unmoved. The front and the back of each line change together, and everything between them holds still.

\textbf{The verb carries the tense.} The day word says which day. Neither is doing the other's work.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of these words were new. \textbf{The third was already yours and you could not use it.}

\textbf{\ml{നാളെ}} had been sitting inside \textbf{\ml{നാളെ} \ml{കാണാം}} since your first week, doing nothing but ending a conversation. A learner who had said that goodbye a hundred times still could not say \emph{tomorrow I will go}, because the word had never been shown standing anywhere else.

That is worth noticing as a habit and not only as a fact: \textbf{a phrase you learned whole may be holding a word you can use apart from it.} When one of them turns out to detach, you gain a word without learning one.

And with these three, \textbf{every sentence you own can now be dated.} The tenses were built chapters ago and had nowhere to land.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{innale}, \emph{innŭ}, \emph{nāḷe} — in that order
  \item \emph{innale ñān pōyi}
  \item \emph{nāḷe ñān pōkuṁ}
  \item which of the three words you already had, and where
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Yesterday, today, tomorrow? (\textbf{\ml{ഇന്നലെ}, \ml{ഇന്ന്}, \ml{നാളെ}}.) Where does a day word stand? (\textbf{In front}.) And what tells you the tense? (\textbf{The verb ending}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
